explain: With rare large losses, the median is often zero. Budgets and control decisions use the mean (the ALE) and reserves or insurance use the tail percentiles.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: ISO/IEC 27001: an ISMS, Annex A and the certification audit
question: Which statement about an ISO/IEC 27001 certificate is true?
options: It proves the company has never been breached
It replaces the need for a risk register
It certifies every product the company sells
It shows an accredited body found the ISMS, within the stated scope, meets the standard's requirements, and it is kept valid by surveillance audits
explain: The certificate is about the management system within its scope. Breaches can still happen; the question is whether risk is being managed systematically.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Compliance as code: policy checks in CI and automatic evidence
question: Why does the checker read `configuration` references instead of matching the encryption resource's `bucket` value in `change.after`?
options: Because `after` is always empty
Because Terraform forbids reading `after`
Because references are faster to parse
Because the bucket id is not known until apply, so `after` has no usable value; the references show which resource the expression points at
explain: In the real plan the encryption resource lists bucket under after_unknown. Terraform's JSON format documents expression references so tools can link resources before apply.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Policies people follow and awareness that works
question: What did the Lain et al. 15-month study find most useful?
options: Embedded training pages after a click
Annual compliance quizzes
Punishing repeat clickers
Employees reporting suspicious emails, which detected new phishing campaigns quickly
explain: Embedded training showed no benefit and possible side effects; crowd-sourced reporting gave fast detection of new campaigns.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: The long tail: why one response can idle a whole cluster
question: A colleague proposes doubling the number of rollout engines, each still decoding a share of one synchronous batch, to fix 51% engine idleness. What is the main flaw?
options: More engines need more weight-sync bandwidth, which is the real bottleneck
Doubling engines doubles the length of every response
Engines cannot run in parallel on one batch
The idle time is set by the longest response, and one response cannot be split across engines, so the phase still lasts as long as that response
explain: Autoregressive decoding of one response is sequential. Adding engines shortens the time to finish the short responses, but the phase still waits for the longest one, so idleness goes up. verl's fully async docs make the same point: in the colocated case, adding rollout resources cannot remove long-tail idleness.

courseTitle: Roofline model and GPU bandwidth measurement
lessonTitle: Why a kernel is limited by its slowest resource
question: A kernel does 2 GFLOP and moves 4 GB on an H100 (989.5 TFLOP/s BF16, 3.35 TB/s). Which change would speed it up the most?
options: Fusing it with the next kernel so its output never goes to DRAM
Switching from BF16 to FP8 Tensor Cores to double the math rate
Raising the SM clock to increase peak FLOP/s
Unrolling the inner loop to improve instruction level parallelism
explain: Math time is 2 GFLOP / 989.5 TFLOP/s = 2 us, memory time is 4 GB / 3.35 TB/s = 1,194 us. The kernel is memory bound, so only cutting bytes (fusion keeps intermediates on chip) helps. Every option that speeds up math leaves the 1,194 us untouched.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: Walking the dependency graph to the anomalous frontier
question: Pricing is anomalous and so is catalog, which pricing calls. A junior engineer proposes rolling back pricing, since pricing is where the user-visible errors are counted. What does the frontier rule say?
options: Roll back pricing: it is the service returning errors, so it owns the symptom
Roll back both at once to save time
Pricing's anomaly is already explained by its anomalous dependency, so it is not a candidate until catalog is ruled out
Neither is a candidate, because both are anomalous
explain: The frontier keeps only anomalous nodes whose dependencies are healthy. Pricing's slowness is fully accounted for by waiting on catalog, and rolling back pricing changes nothing about the catalog queue while adding a second change to reason about. Rolling back both at once also destroys your ability to attribute the recovery to either one.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: Why fuse ranks instead of scores
question: A new BM25 build multiplies every BM25 score by 3 (same order). What happens to the RRF-fused list?
options: Nothing: ranks are unchanged, so every RRF score is unchanged
BM25 now dominates the fusion, like the raw sum
Dense-only documents rise because BM25 is now relatively noisier
The fused list changes only if k is smaller than 3
explain: RRF reads only r(d). Any monotone transformation of one system's scores leaves its ranks, and therefore the fused list, identical. A raw score sum would change; min-max would not change in this case either, but would under a non-linear transform.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Bindings, helpers, abstractions: the layers under a Rust driver
question: A colleague's build fails: `bindings::spin_lock` does not exist even though `spin_lock()` is used all over the C code. Most likely cause?
options: The bindings crate only includes headers listed in `rust/helpers/`
Rust code may not take spinlocks
`spin_lock` is a macro or inline function in C, so bindgen emits no callable symbol; a `rust/helpers/` wrapper is needed
bindgen only runs when `CLIPPY=1` is set
explain: bindgen generates declarations for real functions and types it finds in the headers included from `rust/bindings/bindings_helper.h`. For C inline functions and non-trivial macros the docs say to add a small wrapper to `rust/helpers/`, exactly like `rust_helper_mutex_lock`.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: What Rust in the kernel does not prevent, and what it costs
question: Which of these bugs does the safe `Mutex`/`Guard` API rule out at compile time in a driver that uses no `unsafe`?
options: Taking lock A then B in one path and B then A in another (ABBA deadlock)
Returning from an error path while the mutex is still held
Calling a sleeping function while holding a spinlock
Holding the lock for too long and hurting latency
explain: The guard's `Drop` unlocks on every exit path. Lock ordering is still checked at runtime by lockdep, sleeping in atomic context needs extra tooling such as klint, and latency is a design question no type system answers.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Worked example: weighted vtime fairness in a few lines of BPF
question: You remove the clamp from scx_simple's enqueue. Which symptom appears first?
options: CPU-bound tasks starve each other in a round-robin cycle
A task waking from a long sleep runs back to back for about as long as it slept, starving CPU-bound tasks
The verifier rejects the program because vtime can underflow
Nice values stop having any effect
explain: A sleeper's vtime stays where it was, while running tasks keep advancing. Without the cap, the waker is far behind and wins every pick until it catches up. If that exceeds the watchdog timeout, the scheduler could even be unloaded for stalling others.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Attack surface, and the Morris worm's four doors
question: Which Morris worm door involved no programming bug at all?
options: Trusted-hosts logins and guessable passwords
fingerd reading input with gets()
sendmail's debug command
None: every door was a coding error
explain: Trusted hosts worked exactly as designed, and weak passwords are a human choice. Attack surface includes features and people, not just bugs. The fingerd and sendmail doors were implementation errors.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: EternalBlue and WannaCry: a patch, a leak and a worm
question: An organisation cannot patch an old Windows Server this week. Which CISA fallback reduces the risk most?
options: Disable SMBv1 and block SMB ports at the network boundary
Turn off Windows Update
Rename the server
Pay for a larger internet connection
explain: CISA recommended disabling SMBv1 and blocking TCP 445 and related ports at the boundary when the patch could not be applied. This removes or hides the vulnerable code path.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Who does security work: the job families
question: In the SSH pipeline, why match `from [0-9.]+` instead of taking a fixed word position with awk on the whole line?
options: Because lines for nonexistent users contain two extra words ('invalid user'), so the address is not always in the same position
Because grep is faster than awk
Because awk cannot read log files
Because IP addresses are encrypted in the log
explain: The 'invalid user' variant shifts every later field by two. Matching the text right after 'from' finds the address in both formats.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: When the filter lies: lucky answers, proxy rewards, overfitting
question: In ReST, reward model scores keep rising with every Grow step, but human raters prefer the model after one Grow step. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The policy is increasingly exploiting errors in the learned reward model, a proxy for human judgment
Human raters are noisier than the reward model, so their results should be ignored
The Improve thresholds were set too low
Translation quality cannot improve after one Grow step for any method
explain: The reward model is only a proxy. Optimizing a proxy harder eventually finds outputs it overrates. The ReST authors say exactly this and suggest periodically refreshing the reward model with human labels on the newest policy's outputs.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: What is safe to cache: scoping, context and invalidation
question: Your support bot caches answers for 24 hours with a TTL that refreshes on every hit, as RedisVL does when a TTL is set. The refund policy changes today. What happens to the popular cached answer "Refunds are accepted within 30 days"?
options: It expires within 24 hours of the change
It may never expire, because every hit resets its TTL; you must delete it or bump a version tag
Redis detects that the source changed and evicts it
It expires at midnight
explain: A TTL that refreshes on access measures time since last use, not time since creation. A frequently asked question keeps getting hit and never expires. Policy-dependent answers need explicit invalidation: delete by source id or change the scope version.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: The server as a confused deputy
question: In Hardy's story, what made the compiler a confused deputy?
options: The compiler used its own write permission to act on a file name chosen by the user
A buffer overflow in the compiler
The user stole the administrator's password
The billing file had no permissions at all
explain: The compiler held authority from two sources: the user's request and its own licence to write in its home directory. It applied its own authority to a name the user supplied. The code had no bug in the usual sense.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Egress filtering, isolation and detecting SSRF
question: A webhook feature must call arbitrary customer URLs (OWASP Case 2). Which combination fits best?
options: Block private, loopback and link-local destinations on the resolved IP, run the sender in an isolated network with no internal routes and no credentials, and log egress
An allowlist of customer domains, updated by hand
Trust any URL that uses https
Only allow port 443 and nothing else
explain: Case 2 cannot use an allowlist, so the app blocks internal destinations on the resolved address and the network makes internal targets unreachable anyway. https alone says nothing about the destination; port filtering alone still allows internal web services on 443.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Equifax and Spring4Shell: when the framework evaluates input
question: Why did the 2010 fix for CVE-2010-1622 not prevent Spring4Shell?
options: It blocked specific known paths to the class loader (a denylist), and JDK 9 added a new path through modules that the list did not include
It was never released
It only applied to Python
Spring4Shell used SQL injection
explain: Denylists fail open when the platform changes underneath them. The module system created a new route to the class loader. Binding allowlists, as in the fixed code, do not have this problem.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Detecting server-side attacks and the defence map
question: A team can do only one thing this quarter. Which control reduces the impact of the widest range of server-side attacks, including ones not yet discovered?
options: Default-deny egress from application servers, with an allowlist and logging
A WAF rule for each new CVE
Renaming admin URLs
Disabling HTTP/2
explain: Egress control breaks SSRF to internal hosts, XXE and Log4Shell callbacks and many exfiltration paths, and its denials are evidence. WAF rules lag behind each new variant; renaming URLs is obscurity, not control.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Inside the server: three processes and an overlapped loop
question: Your server runs out of GPU memory during prefill of very long prompts, while decoding is fine. Which change do the docs suggest first?
options: Disable the radix cache
Switch the schedule policy to lpm
Lower `--chunked-prefill-size` (for example to 4096 or 2048)
Increase `--mem-fraction-static`
explain: Prefill activations scale with the number of tokens in one forward pass, and chunking caps it. Raising `--mem-fraction-static` would give the KV pool more memory and leave less for activations, making prefill OOM more likely.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Bidirectional search and contraction hierarchies
question: While contracting v, the path u, v, w costs 8, and a witness search finds a path from u to w avoiding v that also costs 8. What should the preprocessing do?
options: Add the shortcut, because ties must be preserved
Add the shortcut with weight 7 to prefer it
Abort the contraction of v
Skip the shortcut; an equally short path survives without v
explain: A shortcut is only needed when the path through v is the unique shortest path. An equally short witness keeps dist(u, w) correct in the remaining graph. In the toy, contracting G found a witness for D to T that is even shorter (the shortcut of weight 7 beats 8), so no shortcut was added there either.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: Frequency bins, resolution and spectral leakage
question: Audio at 48000 Hz is analyzed with a 4096-point FFT. What is the spacing between frequency bins?
options: About 11.7 Hz
About 0.085 Hz
explain: Bin spacing is fs/N = 48000/4096 = 11.71875 Hz. 24000 Hz is the Nyquist frequency (the last rfft bin), not the spacing. A 4096-sample block lasts about 85 ms, and the spacing is the inverse of that duration.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Writing a vector loop: intrinsics, reductions and tails
question: Clang will not vectorize `for (...) s += a[i];` over floats at -O2, but does vectorize the same loop over ints. Why?
options: Integer SIMD registers are wider
Floats cannot be loaded with vector loads
The loop has an aliasing problem only for floats
Vectorizing changes the order of additions, which changes float rounding but not integer results
explain: Wraparound integer addition is associative, so any order gives the same bits. Float addition rounds at every step, so reordering can change the result, and the compiler needs -ffast-math, -fassociative-math or a pragma to allow it.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Shipping SIMD: -march levels, runtime dispatch, portability
question: In the Rust example, why is `sum_avx2` marked `unsafe`?
options: It dereferences raw pointers
AVX2 instructions are memory-unsafe
Rust forbids SIMD in safe code
Calling it on a CPU without AVX2 would execute unsupported instructions, so the caller must guarantee the feature
explain: The std::arch docs explain that #[target_feature] functions can only be correctly called on systems with that feature, so calling them is unsafe; the is_x86_feature_detected! check is what makes the call sound.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: The slab allocator: caches of ready-made objects
question: Why can the slab allocator reclaim memory without the coalescing step a buddy allocator needs?
options: Because it never returns memory to the system
Because objects are always freed in the order they were allocated
Because a slab is a whole page-sized unit with a refcount: when the count reaches zero the entire slab goes back, no matter where its neighbors are
Because slab objects are always 2^k bytes and aligned like buddies
explain: The slab, not the object, is the unit exchanged with the page allocator. Freeing an object only decrements its slab's count; when it hits zero the slab's pages return in one step.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Moving weights from Megatron into SGLang
question: Your trainer runs with PP=4. In the NCCL path, how many weight-update process groups are created, and who sends in each?
options: One group; global rank 0 gathers everything and sends
One group per engine; every training rank sends its own shard
Four groups, one per pipeline stage; that stage's DP-rank-0, TP-rank-0 rank broadcasts its layers
No groups; SGLang pulls from Megatron's checkpoint
explain: Each pipeline stage holds different layers, so slime creates a group per stage (`slime-pp_{rank}`), and the stage's source rank (data-parallel rank 0, tensor-parallel rank 0) broadcasts full tensors after the TP and EP gathers.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: The alert lifecycle, and why the queue is not first come, first served
question: An analyst tries to close a case with the note "looks fine" and no verdict. Why should the case tool refuse?
options: Because closed cases cannot be reopened
Because without a verdict and a reason, nobody can review the decision or tune the rule, and real attacks dismissed this way are never found
Because every alert must be escalated to Tier 2 before closing
Because notes must be at least 100 characters
explain: The verdict and the evidence-based reason are what quality review and rule tuning run on. "Looks fine" cannot be checked by anyone, which is exactly how alerts get "dismissed without good reason".

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: When the attacker calls the help desk: MFA resets and new devices
question: A help desk resets MFA for a finance clerk at 10:00 after a call. At 10:05 the clerk's account signs in from a new device through an anonymising proxy and creates a mail rule forwarding all mail with "invoice" to an outside address. What do you do first?
options: Close: the help desk ticket shows the reset was authorised
Email the clerk to ask whether they set up the rule
Revoke the sessions and the new factor, remove the forwarding rule, and verify with the clerk by phone on the HR-listed number
Wait for a second alert to confirm
explain: The ticket proves only that someone called. A new device through a proxy within minutes, followed by a forwarding rule aimed at invoices, is classic account takeover. Contain first, then verify out of band. Emailing the account the attacker may control is the wrong channel.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Ransomware precursors, and deciding fast: Colonial Pipeline
question: Colonial shut down the whole pipeline although the ransomware was found on the IT network, not on the systems controlling the pipeline. According to the CEO's testimony, why?
options: Because they did not know where the attack started or how far it had spread, and stopping the pipeline was the surest way to keep it from reaching the OT network
Because the OT network had already been encrypted
Because the ransom note demanded it
Because regulators ordered the shutdown
explain: The testimony says the stop work order aimed to keep the malware from spreading to the OT network "if it had not already", because the origin and scope were unknown. It is a textbook decision under uncertainty, made by people with authority to make it.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: SOAR playbooks: what to automate and what to keep human
question: A playbook automatically blocks at the firewall every source IP that triggers a brute-force alert. What is the main risk?
options: Attackers, or simple misconfigurations, can make it block addresses you depend on, such as shared carrier IPs or partners, turning your own automation into a denial of service
Firewalls cannot block IPs automatically
It makes the SOC too fast
Brute-force alerts are always false positives
explain: The trigger is driven by input others control, and IPs are shared (lesson 5). Bound the action: never-block lists, expiry times, approval for anything that is not clearly hostile and clearly yours to block.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Enforcing sparsity: L1, TopK and JumpReLU
question: An L1 SAE's latents look right on inspection, but its reconstructions are consistently a bit too short (smaller norm than x). What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: Dead latents; resample them
The learning rate is too high; lower it
Shrinkage from the L1 penalty; use TopK, JumpReLU or a Gated SAE, or re-fit magnitudes on the chosen latents
The dictionary is too large; reduce M
explain: L1 pulls every active magnitude down by about lambda/2 (in the one-latent case), so x-hat is systematically small. Architectures that decouple selection from magnitude remove this bias.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: The semivariogram: measuring how similarity decays with distance
question: Your fitted variogram has a large nugget, almost equal to the sill. What does this say about your sensors?
options: Readings are strongly correlated at all distances, so interpolation will be very accurate
The range must be zero, so kriging cannot be run
Even very close sensors disagree about as much as distant ones, so spatial interpolation adds little over the mean
Close sensors always agree exactly
explain: The nugget is the semivariance as distance approaches zero. If it is almost the sill, nearby pairs differ about as much as unrelated pairs: the measurable spatial structure is weak (or dominated by measurement error), and kriging estimates approach the mean.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Why decoding is slow and why checking guesses is cheap
question: Which claim about speculative decoding is correct?
options: It speeds up decoding by letting a smaller model answer the easy prompts
It trades a small amount of quality for latency, like quantization
It produces the same output distribution as the target model and only changes how many target passes are needed
It only works with greedy decoding
explain: Both original papers prove the sampled tokens follow the target's distribution for any draft. Quality is unchanged; speed depends on how well the draft guesses. Lesson 3 covers sampling, not just greedy.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Drafting without a second model: Medusa heads and token trees
question: A tree-attention kernel accidentally uses the ordinary causal mask on the flattened tree. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing; causal masking is a superset of tree masking
Only the position ids are off by one
The pass becomes slower but results are identical
Each node also attends to earlier sibling branches, so the target scores tokens in contexts that never occur and verification becomes wrong
explain: Under a causal mask 'think' would attend to 'It', 'is', 'was' and so on, a context that is not its real prefix. Its distribution is then wrong and so are the accept and reject decisions. The mask must restrict attention to ancestors.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Word error rate: alignments, normalization and fair comparisons
question: A reference has 10 words. The aligned hypothesis has 2 substitutions, 1 deletion and 3 insertions. What is the WER?
explain: WER = (S + D + I) / N = (2 + 1 + 3) / 10 = 60%. Dividing by the hypothesis length (12 words) would give 50%, a common bug. 30% forgets the insertions.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Walking an x86-64 page table, bit by bit
question: A program maps 1 GiB of memory and touches all of it with 4 KiB pages. Roughly how much memory do the last-level page tables alone take?
options: 4 KiB
64 KiB
2 MiB
1 GiB
explain: 1 GiB / 4 KiB = 262,144 page-table entries at 8 bytes each = 2 MiB, which is 512 PTE tables of 4 KiB. With 2 MiB pages the same gigabyte needs just 512 PMD entries, one 4 KiB table.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Difference of means: building a vector from contrast pairs
question: In the toy example, the single-pair direction from pair 4 still classifies all eight activations correctly. Why prefer the mean difference anyway?
options: It is the only direction with unit length
It makes projections of negatives exactly zero
Single-pair vectors cannot be added to the residual stream
It is closer to the true concept direction (cosine 0.991 vs 0.891), so steering along it changes less of everything else
explain: Classification only needs the right sign. Steering adds the whole vector, including its off-concept components. Pair 4's direction has a larger share of noise, so adding it would also push unrelated dimensions. The averaged vector is cleaner.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Two clocks: why sensor readings arrive out of order
question: Which timestamp should you use to decide whether a machine overheated between 14:00:00 and 14:00:10?
options: Processing time at the stream processor
Kafka's append time for the record
The event time the sensor stamped on the reading
The time the database row was written
explain: Only the event time refers to when the physical measurement happened. The other three are processing times at different stages, each shifted by network and queueing delay.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Downsampling, retention and exactly-once vs at-least-once
question: A consumer commits its Kafka offset immediately after reading a batch and before writing results. It crashes mid-write. What semantics did you get?
options: Exactly once
At least once
At most once: the batch's unwritten results are lost
No effect, Kafka rolls back the commit
explain: Committing before processing means on restart the consumer resumes after the batch; anything not yet written is never processed. Kafka's docs describe this as the at-most-once pattern.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Positional encoding, residuals and the full Transformer
question: Which sub-layer holds the most parameters in one base-model encoder layer?
options: Multi-head self-attention, because it has 8 heads
LayerNorm, because it has a gain and bias per dimension
The position-wise feed-forward network, about twice as many as attention
They are equal by design
explain: Attention: 4 x 512^2, about 1.05 million. FFN: 2 x 512 x 2048, about 2.10 million. LayerNorm has only 2 x 512 = 1,024 per instance. Heads split the attention width; they do not add parameters.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Document length normalization: what b controls
question: Under b = 0.75, avgdl = 20, k1 = 1.2, what is K = k1 x B for a 40-token document?
options: 1.2, the same as k1
2.4, because the document is twice the average
0.6, because long documents saturate sooner
explain: B = 0.25 + 0.75 x (40/20) = 1.75, so K = 1.2 x 1.75 = 2.1. It is not 2.4 because only the b share of B scales with length; the (1 - b) share stays fixed. A larger K means the long document needs more occurrences to reach the same factor, not fewer.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Stacking blocks: residuals, pre-LayerNorm, MLP and a tied output head
question: For GPT-2 small, roughly what share of all parameters sits in the MLPs?
options: About 10%
About 23%
About 45%
About 31%
explain: The MLPs have 8C^2 + 5C per block, twice attention's 4C^2 + 4C, totalling 56.67M of 124.44M, which is 45.5%. 23% is attention and 31% is the token embedding table.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Many inputs: partial derivatives and the gradient vector
question: A model has 7 billion parameters and a scalar loss. How many numbers are in the gradient of the loss?
options: 1, because the loss is a single number
7 billion, one partial derivative per parameter
About 49 billion billion (7 billion squared), one per pair of parameters
It depends on the batch size
explain: The gradient has one entry per input to the function: here, one partial derivative per parameter. Pairs of parameters appear in the matrix of second derivatives (the Hessian: each entry differentiates one partial derivative again with respect to another parameter), which is far too large to form for such models.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: how bash really runs your commands
lessonTitle: Expansion and quoting: why rm $f can delete the wrong files
question: In bash, `echo {1,2}-$((3+4))` prints what?
explain: Brace expansion runs first and makes two words, `1-$((3+4))` and `2-$((3+4))`. Arithmetic expansion then evaluates each to 7.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: From one-hot IDs to a trainable embedding table
question: Why do the dense vectors let a model generalize from cat to kitten when one-hot codes do not?
options: Dense vectors have more dimensions, so they hold more information
The dot product of two one-hot vectors is undefined
Nearby inputs produce nearby activations, so what the network learned for one word partly applies to the other
Dense vectors are normalized to length 1
explain: The downstream layers are smooth functions of their input. If kitten's vector is close to cat's, the network's output for kitten is close to its output for cat. One-hot codes have more dimensions, not fewer, and their dot products are well defined (just always 0).

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Beyond words: contrastive learning and failure modes
question: Your product catalog adds thousands of new item IDs every day, and the model uses one learned embedding row per ID. What problem should you expect for brand-new items?
options: Their rows are still at their random initialization because they have received no gradient, so their similarities are meaningless
None, embeddings generalize to any ID
They will all collapse to the zero vector
Their vectors will equal the average of all rows
explain: A row learns only when its ID appears in training. New IDs keep their random initial vectors (in PyTorch drawn from N(0, 1)). Systems handle this cold-start problem by building vectors from content features, the same idea fastText uses with character n-grams.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Batching: sharing each weight read across many users
question: Why does continuous batching improve throughput over static batching?
options: Finished requests free their slot right away and waiting requests join at the next step, so fewer slots sit idle
It makes each decode step faster
It removes the need for a KV cache
It runs prefill and decode on different GPUs
explain: The step time is unchanged; what changes is how full the batch is. Iteration-level scheduling refills slots every iteration instead of waiting for the longest request.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Why memory is slow and how caches hide it
question: With a 3-cycle hit time and a 240-cycle miss penalty, what is the average access time at a 5% miss rate?
options: 12 cycles
15 cycles
243 cycles
8 cycles
explain: 3 + 0.05 x 240 = 3 + 12 = 15 cycles. Note that a 5% miss rate already makes the average access 5x slower than a hit: misses dominate.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Pretraining: next-token loss over trillions of tokens
question: Using C of about 6ND, a 7B-parameter model trained on 2 trillion tokens needs roughly how many FLOPs?
explain: 6 x 7e9 x 2e12 = 8.4e22. The rule ignores attention's context-length term, which Kaplan et al. note is small when the model width is large relative to the context.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Reward over-optimization, best-of-N and modern recipes
question: Best-of-N with N = 64 moves the output distribution how far from the base policy, by the analytic formula?
options: About 0.98 nats
About 4.16 nats
About 64 nats
About 3.18 nats
explain: log 64 - 63/64 = 4.159 - 0.984 = 3.175 nats. KL grows only logarithmically in N, which is why best-of-N is a gentle form of optimization.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: TF-IDF: weighting by frequency and rarity
question: N = 1,000,000 and a term has df = 1,000 and tf = 3 in a document. What is its weight with raw tf, and with sublinear tf 1 + log10(tf)?
explain: idf = log10(1,000,000 / 1,000) = 3. Raw: 3 x 3 = 9. Sublinear: (1 + log10 3) x 3 = 1.477 x 3 = 4.43. Sublinear scaling halves this weight here because three occurrences count as about 1.5.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Addresses and pointers: what int *p actually stores
question: On a 64-bit Linux or macOS machine, `char *c;` What are `sizeof c` and `sizeof *c`?
options: 1 and 1
8 and 8
8 and 1
1 and 8
explain: c is a pointer, and object pointers are 8 bytes on these platforms. *c is the char it would point to, which is 1 byte by definition. sizeof only looks at types, so it is fine to apply it even though c is uninitialized.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Who frees this memory? Ownership and drop
question: A function creates `let s = String::from("hi");` and returns normally without doing anything else with `s`. What happens to the heap bytes?
options: They are freed when the function returns, because `s` (the owner) goes out of scope and is dropped
They leak, because there is no explicit free
They are freed later when the garbage collector runs
They stay allocated until the program exits
explain: Rule 3: when the owner goes out of scope the value is dropped, and dropping a String frees its heap buffer. Rust has no tracing garbage collector, and nothing waits until exit.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Lifetimes: tying a returned reference to its inputs
question: Which signature compiles **without** explicit lifetime annotations?
options: `fn pick(a: &str, b: &str) -> &str`
`fn make() -> &str`
`fn get(&self, key: &str) -> &str` (a method)
explain: Rule 3: the output takes the lifetime of `&self`. Options 1 and 4 have two input lifetimes and no receiver, and option 2 has no input lifetime at all, so elision cannot fill in the output in any of them (E0106).

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: A matrix is a function that moves every vector
question: Is $f(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}$ guaranteed to satisfy $f(2\mathbf{x}) = 2f(\mathbf{x})$ for every matrix $A$?
options: Only if A is square
Only if A is a rotation
Yes, for every matrix A
No, only if A has no negative entries
explain: Each output component is $\sum_j A_{ij}(2x_j) = 2\sum_j A_{ij}x_j$. Scaling passes through any matrix. This is half of the definition of linearity; the other half is $f(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}) = f(\mathbf{x}) + f(\mathbf{y})$.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Mini-batches, cross-entropy gradients and the training loop
question: You switch from batch size 100 to batch size 10,000 on a huge dataset. What happens to one step's gradient estimate?
options: Its standard deviation drops about 10 times while each step costs about 100 times more
It becomes exact
Its standard deviation drops about 100 times, matching the 100 times extra compute
Nothing changes, because the minibatch gradient is unbiased at any batch size
explain: Standard error scales as $\sigma/\sqrt B$: $\sqrt{10000/100} = 10$. Unbiasedness means the estimate is right on average at any batch size, but its noise still depends on $B$. Only the full dataset gives the exact gradient.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: The forward pass: layers as matrix multiplies
question: In the convention $z^l = W^l a^{l-1} + b^l$, what is the shape of $W^2$ for that 784-100-10 network?
explain: $W^l$ has one row per unit in layer $l$ and one column per unit in layer $l-1$: 10 output units by 100 hidden units.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Processes and limited direct execution
question: Why must the instruction that installs the trap table be privileged?
options: Because it is slow and should run only at boot
Because the trap table is stored on disk
Because a user process could otherwise point system calls and interrupts at its own code and take over the machine
Because user programs do not know the system-call numbers
explain: The trap table decides which code runs in kernel mode on every trap and interrupt. If a user program could install its own, it would run arbitrary code with full privilege, defeating all protection. So, like starting the timer, it is restricted to kernel mode.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Probability by counting outcomes, and what conditioning does
question: A model's training set has 1,000 emails: 300 are spam, and 240 of the spam emails contain the word "free". Of the 700 non-spam emails, 70 contain "free". What is P(spam | contains "free")?
options: 0.80, because 240 of 300 spam emails contain free
0.24, because 240 of 1,000 emails are spam with free
About 0.77, because 240 of the 310 emails containing free are spam
0.30, the base rate of spam
explain: Condition on the event you observed: restrict to the 240 + 70 = 310 emails containing "free", of which 240 are spam, so 240/310 = 0.774. Option A is P(free | spam), the reverse conditional, a very common mix-up that the next lesson is about.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Estimating parameters from data: maximum likelihood
question: A language model assigns probability 0.5 to every correct next token in a validation set. What is its average cross-entropy (natural log), and what does minimizing it on training data correspond to?
options: 0.5; minimizing the error rate
About 0.693; maximizing the likelihood of the training tokens
About 0.693; minimizing the variance of the predictions
1.0; maximizing accuracy
explain: Cross-entropy averages -log of the probability given to the correct token: -ln 0.5 = 0.693. Minimizing average negative log-likelihood over the training data is exactly maximum likelihood estimation of the model's parameters.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Fixed budget, best split: IsoFLOP curves
question: Under Chinchilla-style scaling (N and D each proportional to about $C^{0.5}$), your compute budget grows 10x. How should the model size change?
options: Grow about 10x, keeping tokens fixed
Grow about 5.4x
Grow about 3.2x, and tokens about 3.2x too
Stay fixed and train 10x longer
explain: $10^{0.5} \approx 3.16$ for both N and D, and $3.16 \times 3.16 = 10$ recovers the 10x compute. 5.4x is the Kaplan prescription ($10^{0.73}$) from the next lesson. Putting all of it into one knob walks up a wall of the IsoFLOP valley.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Precision, recall, and why accuracy is useless for search
question: A query has exactly 3 relevant documents in the qrels. A perfect system ranks all 3 first. What are its P@10 and R@10?
explain: Recall is 3/3 = 1.0 because every relevant document is retrieved. Precision at 10 counts all 10 slots, and only 3 can ever be relevant, so it is 0.3 even for a perfect ranking. This is why P@k is hard to average across queries with different numbers of relevant documents.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: From token vectors to one sentence vector: pooling and cosine
question: Your vectors are L2-normalized at indexing time and queries are normalized too. A teammate switches the scoring function from cosine to dot product to save time. What happens to the ranking?
options: It is identical, because for unit vectors the dot product equals the cosine
It changes, because dot product favors longer documents
It reverses
It becomes random
explain: Cosine divides the dot product by the two lengths. When both lengths are 1, that division does nothing, so the scores and the ranking are identical. This is exactly why normalizing once is standard practice.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Training BPE: count adjacent pairs, merge the top one, repeat
question: Starting from the initial corpus, suppose newest appeared 9 times instead of 6 (everything else unchanged). Which pair would be merged first?
options: (e, s), still tied with (s, t) and (t, _) at 12
(l, o), because low is the most frequent word
(w, e), which rises to 11
(n, e), because newest is now the most frequent word
explain: Each of (e, s), (s, t), (t, _) becomes $9 + 3 = 12$, and (w, e) becomes $9 + 2 = 11$. The top count is a three-way tie at 12, and the first-seen rule picks (e, s). Word frequency alone does not decide: (l, o) gets 7 and (n, e) gets 9.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Initialization: keeping signals alive through 30 layers
question: A 50-layer ReLU MLP uses weights with $\mathrm{Var}(w) = 1/\text{fan-in}$. Without normalization layers, what do you expect at initialization?
options: Activations shrink by about a factor of 2 in variance per layer, so early-layer gradients become tiny
Activations keep roughly constant scale, since 1/fan-in is the textbook choice
Activations explode because ReLU outputs are always positive
Nothing depends on initialization because Adam rescales every step
explain: Var(w) = 1/n gives g = 1, so the variance factor per layer is g/2 = 1/2. After 50 layers the variance is multiplied by about $2^{-49}$. The backward pass has the same product, so early gradients vanish. Adam, the adaptive optimizer of lesson 2, rescales update sizes, but it cannot repair a forward pass whose signal has already disappeared.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: A debugging recipe: loss at init, overfit one batch, read the curves
question: Training loss keeps falling, but after epoch 12 validation loss rises steadily. What is the recipe's next move?
options: Increase the learning rate to escape the minimum
Re-initialize with He init
Regularize: more data or augmentation, dropout, weight decay, or stop early at the best validation loss
Remove model.eval() so validation uses batch statistics
explain: Diverging train and validation curves are overfitting, which is exactly what stage 4 (regularize) addresses. Early stopping on validation loss keeps the epoch-12 model while you try stronger regularization.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Tuning ef and M, and choosing between HNSW, IVF and PQ
question: You must index 1 billion 768-d vectors on machines with limited RAM. Which choice best fits the constraint?
options: HNSW,Flat, because it has the best recall versus speed
Brute force on GPUs, because it is exact
IVF with PQ codes, because each vector shrinks from 3,072 bytes to around 100
HNSW with a larger M, because more links mean less memory
explain: Raw float32 vectors alone would be about 3 TB, and HNSW,Flat needs them in RAM. IVF,PQ stores about m + 8 bytes per vector (about 104 GB with 96 codes), at some accuracy cost. A larger M increases memory, it does not reduce it.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Typosquatting and dependency confusion: winning by name
question: Why does moving internal packages under an npm scope such as @acme defeat dependency confusion?
options: Scoped names are encrypted
npm refuses to publish scoped packages publicly
Scoped packages cannot have install scripts
A scope maps to exactly one registry, so the resolver never asks the public registry for @acme packages
explain: npm's documentation: scopes have a many-to-one relationship with registries; a scope only ever points to one registry. The public registry is simply not consulted for that name. (Also claim the @acme scope publicly so nobody else can.)

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: CI secrets: Codecov and the keys inside every pipeline
question: Codecov's attacker never touched Codecov's git repository. Why didn't that protect anyone?
options: Git repositories cannot store shell scripts
The attacker deleted the repository
GitHub was also compromised
Customers downloaded the script from a storage bucket at run time, so the bucket was the real source of truth
explain: What runs is what is downloaded, not what is in git. The customer who compared the downloaded script with the published hash checked the right thing.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Provenance and SLSA levels: a signed record of how it was built
question: Which attack does SLSA Build L3 provenance NOT protect against?
options: Uploading a locally built package by hand
Modifying an artifact after the build
A compromised build step forging the provenance
A maintainer committing a backdoor to the main branch, which is then built normally
explain: The build was faithful to the source; the source was bad. That needs the Source track (enforced review) and human scrutiny, which is exactly the xz problem.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: xz-utils II: where the payload hid and how it was caught
question: Which distribution practice would have kept the backdoor out of a package even if the 5.6.1 version was adopted?
options: Verifying the maintainer's signature on the tarball
Running the package's test suite
Using a newer compiler
Building the package from the tagged git source instead of the release tarball
explain: The trigger lived only in the tarball. Arch Linux switched xz to build from git when the backdoor was disclosed. The signature was valid (Jia Tan signed it), and the tests passed.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Replace versus accumulate: what keeps the error bounded
question: Under accumulation with d = 10, T = 100 and noise variance 1, what is the test error after iteration 2?
options: 0.225, twice the first iteration
0.112, unchanged
0.185, the bound
0.140, which is 1.25 times the first iteration
explain: The sum is 1 + 1/4 = 1.25, so the error is 0.1124 x 1.25 = 0.140. Doubling (0.225) is the replace result.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: mmap: putting a file into your address space
question: The 10,000-byte file is mapped writable with MAP_SHARED and length 12,288. You write p[10500] = 'x'. What happens?
options: SIGBUS, because byte 10,500 is past end of file
The file grows to 10,501 bytes
The write succeeds in memory but is never written to the file
SIGSEGV, because shared mappings cannot be written past EOF
explain: Byte 10,500 is in page 2, the last partial page, so it is mapped and zero-filled. mmap(2) says modifications to that tail region are not written out to the file. mmap never changes a file's size; use ftruncate first if you need the file to grow. SIGBUS would only come from touching page 3, which is wholly beyond EOF.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Measuring correctly: intended start times and HdrHistogram
question: Spot the bug in this load loop: `t0 = now(); send(req); resp = recv(); hist.record(now() - t0)` run back to back on 16 connections.
options: It records in milliseconds instead of microseconds
It measures from actual send time on closed-loop connections, so requests delayed while the connection was blocked are never counted
It should use the mean instead of a histogram
Nothing, 16 connections make it open-loop
explain: Each connection only sends after the previous reply, and t0 is taken at actual send. Time a request spent waiting to be sent during a stall is invisible. Fix: drive sends from a rate plan and record now() minus the intended send time.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Merging overlapping roles: union, gaps and double counting
question: In the sweep, `merged[-1][1]` is the end of the last merged block. A developer writes `merged[-1][1] = e` instead of `max(merged[-1][1], e)`. On the toy resume (generous convention), what total does the code report?
options: 132 months, the bug never triggers
180 months, it stops merging
129 months: B, nested inside A, cuts A's block short by 3 months
137 months, gaps are counted
explain: When B (ending Dec 2017) is merged into A's block, the end is overwritten from Mar 2018 to Dec 2017, losing Jan to Mar 2018. C still starts a new block, D and E extend it correctly, so the total is 31 + 98 = 129. Nested intervals are exactly the case max() exists for.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Coverage: how pass@k grows with the number of samples
question: A model has pass@1 = 0.01 on a problem. Roughly how many independent samples give a 63% chance of at least one correct answer?
options: About 10
About 63
About 100
About 1,000
explain: $1 - 0.99^{100} = 0.634$. In general, $k \approx 1/p$ samples give about $1 - 1/e = 63\%$ coverage for small $p$.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Exchanging test-time compute for a bigger model
question: Using Snell et al.'s FLOPs model with M = 14, how much more inference compute can the small model use at R = 1?

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Titans: surprise, momentum and a forget gate for neural memory
question: In the Titans update, the model sets alpha_t close to 1 at some token. What does that do?
options: Writes this token's value with maximum strength
Clears almost all of the memory before adding the current update
Freezes the memory so this token is ignored
Carries all of the previous surprise into this step
explain: alpha_t multiplies the old memory by (1 - alpha_t). Near 1 that wipes the memory, which is useful at a hard context boundary. Write strength is theta_t; carrying past surprise is eta_t.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: Thrashing at the boundary, and why two magazines bound it at 1/M
question: A CPU with loaded-plus-previous magazines (M = 10) runs a burst of 1,000 allocations with no frees, starting with a full loaded magazine and an empty previous one. About how many depot visits does it make?
options: About 1, the previous magazine absorbs the rest
About 100
About 500
About 1,000
explain: One-sided runs are exactly the case the 1/M bound describes. Each depot trip delivers one full magazine of 10 rounds, so 1,000 allocations need roughly 1,000 / 10 = 100 trips (the first 10 come from the magazine already loaded).

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Assets and adversaries: what is worth taking, and by whom
question: Why should a threat model list a support engineer's login as an asset, even though it holds no data itself?
options: Because logins are covered by compliance rules
Because it is a stepping stone that grants access to data the attacker wants
Because support engineers are the most likely attackers
Because every account must be listed for completeness
explain: Access is an asset. A login that can read any user's notes is as valuable to an attacker as the notes themselves. Compliance and completeness are not the reason, and the model makes no claim that support staff are likely attackers.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Attack trees: start from the attacker's goal
question: An AND node has children costing 300 and 700. It sits under an OR node whose other child costs 800. What is the OR node's cost?
explain: The AND node sums: 300 + 700 = 1,000. The OR node takes the cheaper of 1,000 and 800, which is 800.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Case: Target 2013, a vendor login across a trust boundary
question: Which single change would most directly have broken the Target attack path at the start?
options: Encrypting the card database at rest
Faster antivirus updates on POS terminals
Restricting the vendor login so it could reach only the billing system, not the internal network
Requiring Target employees to change passwords monthly
explain: The vendor credential was the first link, and its access beyond billing let the attackers move inward. Encryption at rest would not stop RAM scraping, which reads data in memory; employee password rotation was not the entry point.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: Why memory is becoming a hierarchy of tiers
question: Using the model with DRAM 100 ns and CXL 200 ns, what fraction of accesses must hit DRAM to get an average of 120 ns?
explain: 120 = 100h + 200(1 minus h) = 200 minus 100h, so h = 0.8. Each 1% of accesses moved to CXL adds 1 ns here.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Splitting a series into trend, season and remainder
question: A city's electricity demand used to peak in winter (heating) and now peaks in summer (air conditioning). Which decomposition choice handles this best?
options: Classical decomposition, because it averages each month over all years
A larger moving-average window for the trend
STL with a seasonal component allowed to change over time
Multiplicative classical decomposition
explain: Classical decomposition assumes the same seasonal pattern every year, so it would average the old winter peak with the new summer peak. STL lets the seasonal component evolve, which is exactly what this series needs. FPP3 uses this electricity example to illustrate the limitation.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: What TLS promises, and what it does not
question: Which attacker does TLS assume?
options: Only a passive eavesdropper who records traffic
An attacker with malware on the client machine
An attacker who controls the server
An active network attacker who can read, drop, modify, replay and inject packets
explain: TLS is designed for a fully active attacker on the network path. Malware on an endpoint or a compromised server is outside its threat model, because those see the data before encryption or after decryption.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: TLS 1.2, RSA key exchange and forward secrecy
question: Why does ECDHE give forward secrecy while the server still has a long-term certificate key?
options: The long-term key only signs; session keys come from ephemeral DH values deleted after use, so the long-term key never decrypts anything
The certificate key is rotated every connection
ECDHE uses a longer key
The certificate is encrypted
explain: Forward secrecy comes from separating the roles: signing proves identity, ephemeral DH creates the secret. A stolen signing key lets you forge future handshakes but cannot recompute past DH secrets.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Hostname checks and the code that turns verification off
question: Why is `check_hostname = False` dangerous even when the chain is still verified (CERT_REQUIRED)?
options: It disables encryption
Any valid certificate for any domain, which an attacker can get for their own domain in minutes, would be accepted for this host
It makes the handshake slower
It turns off forward secrecy
explain: Chain validation proves a CA vouched for some name. Without the hostname check, the attacker simply presents a genuine certificate for a domain they own.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Revocation: CRL, OCSP, stapling, and why short-lived certs won
question: A company's server key leaks. Its certificate has 300 days left. Which plan actually limits the damage most?
options: Revoke the certificate and keep using the same key with a new certificate
Do nothing until expiry
Revoke the certificate, generate a new key pair, get a new certificate, and move to automated short-lived certificates
Turn on OCSP stapling
explain: A new certificate on the old key is still usable by the thief. Revocation helps where clients check CRLs, but short lifetimes bound the exposure regardless of how clients check.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: goto fail: one duplicated line that skipped the signature check
question: Which change, applied alone, would have prevented this bug from shipping?
options: A test that connects to a server signing its key exchange with the wrong key and expects the handshake to fail
Switching from SHA-1 to SHA-256
Using longer RSA keys
Enabling OCSP
explain: The code passed every test with valid servers because valid signatures and skipped checks look the same. Only a negative test (bad input must be rejected) exposes a check that never runs.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Fused softmax: one row per program, reductions on chip
question: Why does the fused softmax kernel move about 4x fewer bytes than the five-op PyTorch version?
options: Triton compresses data before writing it to DRAM
Intermediates (max, shifted values, exponentials, sums) stay in registers instead of round-tripping through DRAM
Triton uses fp16 automatically
The fused kernel skips the max subtraction
explain: Each separate op reads its input from DRAM and writes its output back. Fusing keeps all intermediates on chip, leaving one read and one write of the matrix: 2MN instead of 8MN + 4M elements.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Everything is a token: Chameleon and Emu3
question: A product team wants a Chameleon-style model to read dense receipts and screenshots. What is the main risk the Chameleon paper itself points to?
options: Next-token prediction cannot model 2D layouts at all
The model cannot attend from text to image tokens
The vocabulary has no room for more image codes
The discrete tokenizer reconstructs text-heavy images poorly, which upper-bounds OCR quality
explain: With 13 bits per token and 1024 tokens per 512 px image, fine glyph detail is the first thing lost. The paper calls this a core weakness that bounds OCR-heavy tasks. Separate understanding encoders (lesson 5) are one answer.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: One app, two isolation layers: why a whole OS is redundant
question: Why did library operating systems from the 1990s, such as Exokernel, never see wide deployment, while unikernels can run on public clouds?
options: Their libraries were written in unsafe languages
They had to support many kinds of real hardware; a hypervisor exposes a few standard virtual devices instead
They required multicore CPUs that did not exist yet
Hypervisors run library OSes faster than bare metal does
explain: The Mirage paper's argument: libOSes struggled with real-world hardware support. A hypervisor's virtual devices (netfront, blkfront, virtio) are a small, stable target, so only a few simple drivers are needed.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Specializing further, and what you give up
question: Which service is the weakest candidate for a unikernel?
options: A stateless HTTP API that must cold-start in milliseconds per request burst
A DNS server facing the internet where attack surface matters
A UDP packet processor that needs millions of packets per second per core
A CI build runner that shells out to compilers, git and test scripts in many child processes
explain: The build runner depends on fork, exec and many separate programs, which a single-process, single-address-space unikernel does not support. The other three match unikernel strengths: fast boot, small attack surface and low-level I/O specialization.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Durability and memory tiers: WAL, mmap and disk-based ANN
question: Your 768-d fp32 index needs 31 GB and the machine has 16 GB for page cache. Which change most directly attacks the latency cliff?
options: Switch the vectors to the cached tier so they are pre-loaded at startup
Use a faster SIMD instruction set
Increase the number of segments
Compress the vectors (for example to int8 or PQ codes) so the navigation data fits in RAM, and re-rank with full vectors
explain: Pre-loading cannot fit 31 GB into 16 GB, and SIMD speed is irrelevant when waiting on the SSD. Shrinking what the search touches per hop, and reading exact vectors only for the final re-rank, is exactly the DiskANN-style pattern.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: 3D-HybridEngine: resharding the actor with zero redundancy
question: In the naive grouping on 8 GPUs (train 1-4-2, gen 1-2-2-2), why must G2 keep extra memory after the transition?
options: G2 is a pipeline boundary and must buffer activations
Its generation half (q3+q4) does not contain its training quarter (q2), so q2 must be kept for the next training stage
G2 hosts the controller
Consecutive grouping doubles the KV cache on even ranks
explain: Under consecutive TP grouping, G2 is rank 1 of [G1,G2] and gets q3+q4. Its training shard q2 is not inside that, so it must be stored separately until training resumes. The paper marks G2, G3, G6 and G7 as the GPUs with this redundancy.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Shrinking each frame: spatial pooling, SlowFast and time positions
question: Video-ChatGPT keeps T + N tokens by averaging over space and over time separately. Which question is it worst at?
options: What objects appear in the video?
Is the video indoors or outdoors?
Did the person pick up the cup before or after opening the door?
What is the overall topic of the video?
explain: The N spatial tokens are averaged over all frames, and the T temporal tokens are each one averaged vector per frame. Fine spatial detail tied to a specific moment is blurred, which hurts ordering questions about small actions.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: Tokenizing video and attending in space, then in time
question: Keep S = 256 tokens per frame and double the clip from 16 to 32 frames. What happens to the attention pair counts?
options: Every term doubles, so the ratio stays at 15.1
Spatial pairs double to 2,097,152, temporal pairs quadruple to 262,144, full attention quadruples to 67,108,864
Spatial pairs quadruple and temporal pairs double
Nothing changes because attention is per frame
explain: Spatial is T S squared, linear in T. Temporal is S T squared, quadratic in T but small while T is much less than S. Full is (TS) squared. The ST total is 2,359,296, so the advantage grows to TS/(S+T) = 28.4x.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: Measuring world models, and where Genie 2 and 3 go next
question: A team wants to train an RL agent for an Atari game cheaply using imagined experience, and they can collect actions and rewards by playing. Which approach fits best?
options: A model-based RL world model trained on their own action-labelled transitions, such as DreamerV3 or DIAMOND
A Genie-style model trained on unlabelled internet video, since labels are unnecessary
A text-to-video model prompted with the game's name
No world model: imagined experience cannot train agents
explain: When actions and rewards are available, action-conditioned world models built for RL (DreamerV3's latent imagination, DIAMOND's diffusion model with an Atari 100k mean HNS of 1.46) are the direct fit. Genie's latent actions solve a different problem: learning control from video with no labels.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: Linear probe, LoRA or full fine-tune: choosing what to train
question: A hospital fine-tunes an ImageNet-21k ViT on 3,000 X-rays from scanner A; it will be deployed on scanner B, which produces visibly different images. Which plan best matches the evidence in this lesson?
options: Full fine-tune with a randomly initialized head, since it has the highest in-distribution accuracy
Train only the position embeddings
LP-FT: fit the head on frozen features first, then fine-tune all layers
Skip training and use the ImageNet head directly
explain: Deployment shift is exactly where Kumar et al. found fine-tuning from a random head loses to probing, and where LP-FT won on 10 of 10 OOD datasets. The ImageNet head predicts ImageNet classes, and position embeddings alone cannot learn new classes.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: Why per-step tokens break at 50 Hz, and how FAST compresses them
question: A bimanual robot (14 action dims) runs at 50 Hz. How many tokens does per-step 256-bin tokenization need for a 1-second chunk?
explain: 14 dims x 50 steps = 700 tokens, matching the FAST paper's shirt-folding row. FAST needed about 53 for the same chunk.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Vector quantization: snap each vector to its nearest code
question: In the VQ-VAE loss, which parameters receive gradient from the middle term $\lVert \mathrm{sg}[z_e] - e \rVert^2$?
options: The encoder only
The decoder only
Both the encoder and the codebook
The codebook only
explain: sg blocks the gradient to z_e, so only the codebook vectors e are updated by this term. The paper states: the decoder optimises the first term, the encoder the first and last, and the embeddings the middle term.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Token budgets: bits per image, 1D tokenizers and early fusion
question: You can either double the codebook from 8192 to 16,384 codes or halve the number of image tokens from 1024 to 512. Which choice reduces the stage 2 transformer's attention compute more, and why?
options: Doubling the codebook, because a larger softmax is the dominant cost
They are equivalent, since both change bits per image by the same factor
Halving tokens, because attention pairs scale with the square of sequence length while codebook size adds only one bit per token
Neither changes compute
explain: Halving T cuts attention pairs by 4x and bits per image by 2x. Doubling K adds 1 bit per token (13 to 14) and enlarges the embedding and output layers, but leaves sequence length, and thus attention cost, unchanged.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: Mixed prefill and decode in one forward pass
question: A model mixes a backend that reports `reorder_batch_threshold = 1` with one that reports `None`. Does the runner reorder?
options: No, because None disables reordering for everyone
Yes, but each backend gets its own differently ordered copy of the batch
Yes, with threshold 1. The runner takes the minimum and ignores None
Only on steps that contain no prefills
explain: `calculate_reorder_batch_threshold` reduces with a min that skips None. One batch order is shared by all layers, so the smallest threshold wins, and backends that need no order are unaffected.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Small text needs pixels: AnyRes tiling and dynamic resolution
question: Qwen2-VL's model card says the default visual-token range is 4 to 16,384 per image and suggests setting max_pixels to 1280 x 28 x 28 to save memory. What happens to a 12-megapixel phone photo under that setting?
options: It is resized, keeping its aspect ratio, so that it fits the pixel budget, and costs about 1,230 tokens instead of about 15,500
It is rejected because it exceeds max_pixels
It is cut into 336 x 336 tiles and every tile is kept
Nothing changes because Qwen2-VL uses native resolution
explain: The resize rule scales the image down, preserving aspect ratio, until it fits within max_pixels, then rounds each side to a multiple of 28. A 3024 x 4032 photo becomes 840 x 1148: 1,230 merged tokens plus 2 markers. Native resolution only holds inside the configured pixel range.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Consensus numbers: which primitives can build wait-free objects
question: Why does a failed compare&swap make the consensus protocol work for any number of processes, while a lost test&set does not?
options: CAS is faster than test&set on modern hardware
CAS uses more memory, so it can store all inputs
test&set is not atomic
A failed CAS returns the stored value, which is the winner's input; a lost test&set returns only a bit
explain: The losers' problem is identifying the winner. CAS writes the winner's value into the shared word and hands it back to every loser. test&set returns 1 to every loser and carries no identity.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Why learn the weather from 80 years of reanalysis
question: A 0.25 degree latitude-longitude grid covers 90N to 90S. Why does it have 721 rows instead of 720?
options: Because ERA5 adds one row of padding for convolutions
Because both poles are grid rows, so there are 720 intervals and 721 edges
Because the equator is stored twice, once per hemisphere
Because 721 is required to make the grid divisible by 4
explain: 180 degrees divided by 0.25 gives 720 intervals; counting the endpoints 90N and 90S gives 721 rows. Longitude wraps around, so 0 and 360 are the same column and there are exactly 1440.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Uncertainty: GenCast's diffusion ensembles and CRPS
question: Why does GenCast start each forecast step from fresh noise rather than from the previous step's output plus a small perturbation?
options: Diffusion models cannot accept conditioning inputs
Sampling from noise each step lets the model draw a new plausible state from the learned conditional distribution, giving sharp, distinct members
Noise makes the model run faster on TPUs
It removes the need for ERA5 initial conditions
explain: The diffusion model represents p(X(t+1) given X(t), X(t-1)). Each fresh noise draw yields a different sample of that distribution, so trajectories diverge realistically. The previous states still enter as conditioning, and forecasts still start from ERA5 plus perturbations.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: The same-origin policy: what it blocks and what it lets through
question: Which statement about the same-origin policy is true?
options: It prevents other sites from sending POST requests to your server
It stops script injected into your own pages from reading your cookies
It keeps localStorage separate per origin
It applies only to https pages
explain: Storage such as localStorage and IndexedDB is partitioned by origin. SOP does not stop cross-origin writes such as form POSTs, does nothing against script running inside your origin (XSS), and applies to http and https alike.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: CORS with credentials, and the misconfigurations that leak data
question: An API trusts any origin that fully matches the regular expression `https://.*example\.com`. Which origin would it wrongly trust?
options: https://app.example.com
https://example.com
https://hackersexample.com
http://app.example.com
explain: The .* before example.com matches any characters, including none and including no dot, so hackersexample.com matches. The http origin fails because the pattern requires https. Exact comparison against a list avoids both mistakes.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: HTTPS, mixed content and HSTS: keeping the network out
question: A site sends `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000` in a response served over plain HTTP. What does the browser do?
options: Stores the host as HSTS for a year
Stores it but only for the current session
Ignores the header, because HSTS is only accepted over HTTPS
Upgrades this one response to HTTPS
explain: Browsers ignore HSTS sent over HTTP. Otherwise a MitM could inject a header for a site that does not support HTTPS (locking users out) or strip and replace it. The header must arrive over a secure connection to count.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: The map: which bug class gets around which rule
question: Which pairing of bug class and the rule it gets around is correct?
options: Clickjacking gets around CSP script-src
Firesheep got around Site Isolation
CORS misconfiguration is a server telling the browser to relax the same-origin policy for the wrong origin
postMessage bugs are fixed by HSTS
explain: A CORS misconfiguration is the site itself switching off SOP's read protection for origins it should not trust. Clickjacking abuses embedding (fixed by framing headers), Firesheep abused unencrypted transport (fixed by HTTPS, Secure and HSTS), and postMessage bugs need code fixes.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: Access tokens and the access check: how Windows says yes or no
question: Which of these is a privilege (in the token) rather than a permission (in an object's DACL)?
options: Read access on the Reports folder for the Sales group
Deny Write on a registry key for Guests
Full control on a service for Administrators
Debug programs (SeDebugPrivilege)
explain: Privileges such as SeDebugPrivilege are listed in the access token and apply across the system. The others are ACEs on particular objects.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: LSASS: why attackers dump its memory, and how Windows protects it
question: A server was fully patched against EternalBlue, yet NotPetya still infected it. According to CISA, what is the most likely route?
options: A zero-day in NTFS
Clearing the Security log
A UAC prompt the admin accepted
Credentials stolen from LSASS on another machine, then used with PsExec or WMIC
explain: CISA describes credential theft with a modified Mimikatz plus PsExec or WMIC as NotPetya's first and most effective method. Patches do not stop valid credentials.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: Sysmon and Microsoft Defender: deeper telemetry, built-in defence
question: You want to know which program opened lsass.exe at 02:10 last night. Which source is designed for that?
options: Security event 4720
Defender event 5007
System event 7045
Sysmon event 10 (ProcessAccess)
explain: Sysmon's ProcessAccess event records one process opening another, and Microsoft's documentation names reading LSASS memory as the use case. It needs a config that includes it, with filters for noise.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: First look at domains and Active Directory
question: Why do attackers who land on one workstation in a domain usually aim for Domain Admins rather than staying local?
options: Local admin rights do not exist in a domain
Domain Admins accounts have no SID
Kerberos is turned off for local accounts only
Domain Admins members can control every machine in the domain, so one account gives the whole network
explain: Domain Admins (RID 512) can administer every domain-joined machine and the DCs. Getting there turns one foothold into control of the organisation.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Why a captured handshake allows offline password guessing
question: An attacker has recorded one WPA2-Personal handshake. Which defence actually slows their offline guessing?
options: Turning on the AP's lockout after 5 failed logins
Hiding the SSID
Having chosen a passphrase with many more bits of randomness
Rebooting the AP
explain: Offline guessing never touches the AP, so lockouts and reboots do nothing, and the SSID is already in the recording. Only the size of the space the passphrase was drawn from, and the per-guess cost, set the attacker's time.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: KRACK and FragAttacks: when the standard itself is wrong
question: Why does reinstalling an in-use key break CCMP's security, even though the key itself stays secret?
options: It disables the MIC
The reinstall reveals the key on the air
It resets the packet counter used as the nonce, so frames are encrypted under the same key and nonce again, repeating keystream
It downgrades CCMP to WEP
explain: CCMP (like any counter-mode scheme) is safe only while key and nonce pairs never repeat. Resetting the counter to 1 under the same key repeats them. It is the same keystream reuse that broke WEP in lesson 2.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: iOS: code signing, sandbox, Secure Enclave and BlastDoor
question: Why did Apple add exponential restart throttling to BlastDoor and imagent?
options: Because Swift crashes more often
To save battery
Because many zero-click exploits need to crash a service many times (for example to break ASLR); doubling the restart delay stretches minutes into hours
To stop spam
